OIIX.name: FIR Tehran
OIIX.conflictType: Interstate conflict — Iran vs Israel/US (fragile ceasefire)
OIIX.narrative: EASA's CZIB-2026-04 reflects a ceasefire that has held since April 2026 but remains fragile, with an elevated Iranian air-defence posture that raises the risk of civil aircraft being misidentified. EASA has warned escalation could resume with little notice. The eastern part of the FIR was partially reopened in June 2026 while the western part remains closed; very few international operators are using it. Most Europe-Asia traffic continues to route south via Egypt/Saudi or north via the Caucasus/Afghanistan. The shoot-down of Ukraine International Airlines flight 752 over Tehran in Jan 2020 illustrates how quickly the situation can deteriorate.

cross.detail: July 2026: The US-Iran ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action and attacks around the Strait of Hormuz. EASA's CZIB continues to advise operators not to operate in the OIIX/Tehran FIR at any altitude. Several states maintain warnings against operations in Iranian airspace. Iran has previously operated advanced air defence and conducted missile activity close to busy international routes with little warning. Major events: June 2026: Iran partially reopened the eastern part of the OIIX/Tehran FIR; western part remains closed. March 2026: OIIX/Tehran FIR closed following large-scale US and Israeli strikes on Iranian military targets and subsequent Iranian missile and drone retaliation. June 2025: Israel and Iran exchanged missile strikes, prompting renewed airspace warnings. Oct 2024: Israel and Iran carried out missile attacks against each other, leading most international operators to avoid both airspaces. Jan 2020: Iran shot down Ukraine International Airlines flight 752 over Tehran after misidentifying the aircraft as a hostile target.

ORBB.name: FIR Baghdad
ORBB.conflictType: Non-state armed groups (IBMGs) + Iranian missile/drone spillover
ORBB.narrative: Despite the regional ceasefire, EASA cites recurrent Iranian drone and ballistic-missile strikes reaching Iraqi airspace, alongside the continued presence of Iranian-backed militant groups (IBMGs), as reasons the Baghdad FIR remains a do-not-operate zone. Iraqi airspace remains technically open to overflights and some operators continue using it, but most Europe-Asia traffic routes south via Egypt/Saudi or north via the Caucasus/Afghanistan. Risks include missile and drone activity, misidentification by air-defence systems operated by local and foreign military forces, and MANPADS held by terrorist groups.

cross.detail: July 2026: The US-Iran ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action and attacks around the Strait of Hormuz. EASA's CZIB continues to advise operators not to operate in the ORBB/Baghdad FIR at any altitude. Several states maintain airspace warnings for Iraq. Major events: June 2026: ORBB/Baghdad FIR reopened to overflights following the US-Iran ceasefire, with north-south routes available. March 2026: ORBB/Baghdad FIR closed following US and Israeli strikes on Iran and subsequent Iranian retaliation. June 2025: Airspace closed following Israeli missile attack on Iran; missiles and drones transited Iraqi airspace. Apr 2024: Airspace closed due to Iranian drone and missile strike on Israel. Apr 2023: Several drone and missile attacks in northern Iraq launched from Turkey and Iran, including strikes near ORSU and ORER. Oct 2021: US operators permitted to overfly the ORBB/Baghdad FIR above FL320 under updated FAA restrictions.

OLBB.name: FIR Beirut
OLBB.narrative: A Trilateral Framework Agreement between Israel, Lebanon and the US (26 June 2026) is a step toward consolidating the ceasefire, but EASA notes its long-term implementation is uncertain, and that Lebanon has not shown it can proactively manage airspace risk. Israeli airstrikes in Lebanon have continued despite repeated ceasefire extensions, and most international operators avoid the airspace. Some states allow limited operations to OLBA/Beirut provided arrivals and departures remain over the Mediterranean Sea. GNSS spoofing and jamming have been reported in the FIR since Nov 2023.

cross.detail: July 2026: The US-Iran ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action and attacks around the Strait of Hormuz. Israeli airstrikes in Lebanon continue and most international operators avoid the OLBB/Beirut FIR. EASA's CZIB continues to advise operators not to operate at any altitude. Several states maintain long-standing warnings. Major events: July 2026: EASA's CZIB continues to advise operators not to operate in the OLBB/Beirut FIR at any altitude following renewed military activity. Feb–Jul 2026: Israeli airstrikes continued in Lebanon despite repeated ceasefire extensions. Oct 2024: Israel launched a ground operation against Hezbollah in southern Lebanon. Nov 2023 – ongoing: GNSS spoofing and jamming reported in the OLBB/Beirut FIR.

OJAC.name: FIR Amman
OJAC.conflictType: Missile/drone overflight risk (regional spillover, no direct conflict on Jordanian soil)
OJAC.narrative: Jordan's airspace has repeatedly seen Iranian missiles and drones pass through en route to other targets, intercepted by Jordanian and allied air defences. Jordanian authorities have not published any airspace restrictions of their own despite this activity. The FIR remains open and operating normally. EASA has issued an Information Note advising operators to factor the potential risk into their assessments before operating in the OJAC/Amman FIR.

cross.detail: July 2026: The US-Iran ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action and attacks around the Strait of Hormuz. Jordan airspace (the OJAC/Amman FIR) remains open and operating normally. The primary risk is missile and drone activity linked to regional conflicts. Major events: July 2026: EASA issued a new Information Note advising operators to take the potential risk into account before operating in the OJAC/Amman FIR following renewed military activity in the Gulf. Feb–Jul 2026: Jordan remained open throughout the Iran conflict, although missile and drone activity affected several neighbouring countries. Apr 2024: Jordan temporarily closed its airspace during the Iranian drone and missile attack on Israel. Oct 2023: Jordan intercepted drones and missiles transiting its airspace during regional escalation.

OKAC.name: FIR Kuwait
OKAC.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OKAC.narrative: Kuwait hosts major US military facilities, making it a plausible target for Iranian retaliation and increasing the risk of civil aircraft being caught up in an attack or an air-defence response. The FIR is currently open for arrivals and departures only; overflights remain prohibited. Missile and drone strikes damaged OKKK/Kuwait airport in March 2026.

cross.detail: July 2026: The US-Iran ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action and attacks around the Strait of Hormuz. The OKAC/Kuwait FIR is open for arrivals and departures only; overflights remain prohibited. EASA's CZIB advises operators not to operate at any altitude. Major events: July 2026: EASA issued a new CZIB advising operators not to operate in the OKAC/Kuwait FIR at any altitude. Feb–Jul 2026: OKAC/Kuwait FIR closed and reopened several times during the Iran conflict. March 2026: Missile and drone strikes damaged OKKK/Kuwait airport. June 2025: Israel and Iran exchanged missile strikes across the region.

OBBB.name: FIR Bahrain
OBBB.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OBBB.narrative: As with Kuwait and Qatar, the US military presence in Bahrain is the main driver of EASA's risk assessment for this FIR. Bahrain lies close to several key military facilities in the Gulf region. The FIR has closed and reopened several times during the Iran conflict before returning to normal overflight operations, but EASA's CZIB continues to advise against operations at any altitude.

cross.detail: July 2026: The US-Iran ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action and attacks around the Strait of Hormuz. Bahrain airspace (the OBBB/Bahrain FIR) remains open to overflights. EASA's CZIB advises operators not to operate at any altitude. Major events: July 2026: EASA issued a new CZIB advising operators not to operate in the OBBB/Bahrain FIR at any altitude. Feb–Jul 2026: OBBB/Bahrain FIR closed and reopened several times during the Iran conflict before returning to normal overflight operations. March 2026: Iranian missile and drone attacks targeted several Gulf states, including incidents affecting airspace around Bahrain. June 2025: Israel and Iran exchanged missile strikes, prompting renewed airspace warnings across the region.

OTDF.name: FIR Doha
OTDF.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OTDF.narrative: Qatar hosts significant US forces and has itself been targeted by Iranian strikes during the recent escalation, keeping it on EASA's do-not-operate list even as operational conditions ease. The FIR has closed and reopened several times during the Iran conflict before returning to largely normal operations; a missile strike was reported at Al Udeid Air Base near Doha in March 2026.

cross.detail: July 2026: The US-Iran ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action and attacks around the Strait of Hormuz. Qatar airspace (the OTDF/Doha FIR) remains open and operating largely normally. EASA's CZIB advises operators not to operate at any altitude. Major events: July 2026: EASA issued a new CZIB advising operators not to operate in the OTDF/Doha FIR at any altitude. Feb–Jul 2026: OTDF/Doha FIR closed and reopened several times during the Iran conflict before returning to normal overflight operations. March 2026: Iranian missile strike reported at Al Udeid Air Base near Doha. June 2025: Israel and Iran exchanged missile strikes, prompting renewed airspace warnings across the region.

OMAE.name: FIR Emirates
OMAE.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OMAE.narrative: The UAE's proximity to the Strait of Hormuz and its role as a regional hub keep it firmly within EASA's risk assessment, despite being operationally busy.

OOMM.name: FIR Muscat — west of 58°E only
OOMM.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OOMM.narrative: Unlike other Gulf FIRs, only the western portion of Omani/Gulf of Oman waters is covered — reflecting where commercial vessel attacks and Strait of Hormuz tension actually concentrate. Oman itself remained open throughout the Iran conflict and became a key part of the main southern bypass route (Egypt-Saudi-Oman) used by operators avoiding the closed central Middle East corridor.

cross.detail: July 2026: The US-Iran ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action and attacks around the Strait of Hormuz. Oman airspace (the OOMM/Muscat FIR) remains open and carries significant Europe-Asia overflight traffic on the southern bypass route. EASA's CZIB advises operators not to operate over the waters of the Gulf of Oman within the OOMM/Muscat FIR west of 58°E. Major events: July 2026: EASA issued a new CZIB advising operators not to operate over the waters of the Gulf of Oman within the OOMM/Muscat FIR west of 58°E. Feb–Jul 2026: Oman remained open throughout the Iran conflict and became a key part of the main southern bypass route. June 2025: Israel and Iran exchanged missile strikes, prompting renewed airspace warnings across the Gulf region. Oct 2024: Israel and Iran carried out missile attacks against each other, leading many operators to avoid airspace between the two countries.

OSTT.name: FIR Damascus
OSTT.narrative: EASA's longest-running Middle East bulletin (19 revisions since 2017) reflects a still-unresolved multi-actor conflict. Traffic patterns have shifted: OSTT quietly reopened to some regional carriers in early 2025 as an alternative to the more restricted Iran/Iraq corridor, even though most Western operators continue to avoid it. Risks include Israeli airstrikes targeting Iranian and Hezbollah-linked positions and misidentification by air-defence systems. The FIR closed again in March 2026 following US and Israeli strikes on Iran, before a gradual increase in overflights resumed.

cross.detail: July 2026: The US-Iran ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action and attacks around the Strait of Hormuz. Syrian airspace (the OSTT/Damascus FIR) remains high risk, but some regional operators have started using it as an alternative to the more restricted Iran/Iraq routing. Several countries continue to prohibit or advise against operations due to risk from military operations, anti-aviation weaponry and unstable security conditions. Major events: March 2026: OSTT/Damascus FIR closed following US and Israeli strikes on Iran and subsequent Iranian retaliation. Jan–Jul 2026: Gradual increase in overflights through Syria as some regional operators use the FIR as an alternative to Iran and Iraq. Dec 2024: Syrian airspace temporarily closed following the fall of the Assad regime. Oct 2023: Airstrikes damaged runways at OSDI/Damascus and OSAP/Aleppo airports. Feb 2020: An A320 approaching Damascus diverted after being caught in crossfire during Israeli airstrikes. Sep 2018: Russian IL-20 shot down in error near the Syria-Cyprus FIR boundary.

OYSC.name: FIR Sana'a only
OYSC.conflictType: Civil war + interstate spillover (Red Sea attacks)
OYSC.narrative: This bulletin covers only the Sana'a FIR, not the whole of Yemen. The ongoing civil war and Houthi involvement in the wider regional conflict keep the risk assessment unchanged since 2017. Several countries prohibit aircraft from overflying any land portion of the FIR; US operators can use offshore routes UT702 and M999, while other countries permit flights on overwater portions. OYSN/Sanaa Airport has been closed since damage from Israeli airstrikes in Dec 2024 and May 2025.

cross.detail: Yemen remains an active conflict zone. The primary risks are intentional targeting by terrorist groups with sophisticated anti-aircraft weaponry, high-intensity military operations including explosive drones and missiles, and Saudi and Israeli airstrikes that can occur at any time. Saudi airspace to the north and Somali airspace to the south also carry risks. Major events: Jul 2026: Yemen's government carried out an airstrike on the runway at OYSN/Sanaa Airport to stop an Iranian aircraft from landing. Dec 2024 – ongoing: OYSN/Sanaa Airport closed due to damage from Israeli airstrikes in Dec 2024 and May 2025. Jan 2024: US and UK carried out airstrikes against Houthi rebels in Yemen in response to missile and drone attacks in the Red Sea. Sep 2023: Houthi drone attacks near the Yemen-Saudi border. Apr–Oct 2022: All parties in the Yemeni conflict agreed a ceasefire. 2018–2022: Frequent Saudi airstrikes on Sanaa and other targets in retaliation for Houthi drone attacks. 2017: OYSN/Sanaa Airport badly damaged by coalition airstrikes.

UUWV.name: FIR Moscow and others (west of 60°E)
UUWV.conflictType: Interstate war — Russian invasion of Ukraine (air-defence risk)
UUWV.narrative: Issued after the likely accidental shoot-down of Azerbaijan Airlines flight 8243 near Grozny in December 2024, this bulletin reflects the risk that Russian air-defence systems responding to Ukrainian strikes pose to civil aircraft, compounded by widespread GNSS interference. Drone attacks across Russia have been increasing in frequency and geographic reach, with some reaching as far as Siberia. Russian surface-to-air missiles used to counter Ukrainian drones are capable of reaching all altitudes, making the risk applicable at every flight level. Most activity occurs at night but daytime disruptions are now common. Moscow-area airports have been forced to close temporarily on multiple occasions.

cross.detail: As of June 2025, drone attacks across Russia are ramping up, with some reaching as far as Siberia. Russian air-defence surface-to-air missiles are capable of reaching all altitudes, so the risk applies at every level. Ukraine's airspace has remained fully closed to civil aviation since Feb 2022. Several countries prohibit their operators from using Russian airspace near FIR boundaries with Ukraine due to the persistent risk of misidentification. Major events: Jan 2025: EASA issued a new CZIB recommending against flights in western Russia (anywhere west of 60°E) due to the threat of anti-aircraft fire and high risk of misidentification by air-defence systems targeting Ukrainian drones and missiles, following the shoot-down of a passenger jet at URMG/Grozny on Dec 25. Jan 2024: Crash of a military transport aircraft in Russian airspace near Belgorod, approx 20nm from the Ukrainian border. Aug 2023: The private jet carrying Wagner mercenary chief Yevgeny Prigozhin crashed en route from Moscow to St Petersburg on Aug 23. Jul 2023 – ongoing: Multiple drone strikes on targets in Moscow and surrounding region, forcing temporary airport closures; events are becoming more frequent.

UKBV.name: All Ukrainian FIRs
UKBV.narrative: In force since the day of the invasion, this remains one of the clearest and most stable prohibitions in this dataset — Ukraine itself has closed its FIRs to civil traffic by NOTAM. All major countries that regularly issue airspace warnings (the US, UK, Canada, France, Germany, Italy) have issued total flight bans for Ukraine. Russia, Belarus and Moldova have also closed large sections of their own airspace near their FIR boundaries with Ukraine. Primary risks include misidentification by military systems (as with MAS17 and UIA752), loss of ATC service at short notice (e.g. cyber attack), and other unforeseeable non-normal operating environments.

cross.detail: Ukraine closed its entire airspace to all civil traffic on Feb 24, 2022, due to a military invasion by Russia. All major countries that regularly issue airspace warnings have since issued total flight bans. Russia, Belarus and Moldova have closed large sections of their own airspace near FIR boundaries with Ukraine. Prior to February 2022, two areas of concern existed: the conflict in the far east (affecting UKDV/Dnipro FIR) and the disputed ATC and airspace authority over Crimea (UKFV/URFV/Simferopol FIR).

HSSS.name: FIR Khartoum
HSSS.conflictType: Civil war — Sudan Armed Forces (SAF) vs Rapid Support Forces (RSF)
HSSS.narrative: The ongoing SAF–RSF civil war has put anti-aircraft artillery, MANPADS and SAM systems into play across the whole of Sudanese airspace, keeping the entire Khartoum FIR off-limits. HSSK/Khartoum airport is closed with no NOTAMs being issued; a Contingency Plan with published overflight routes via HSPN/Port Sudan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and South Sudan is available. South Sudan's air navigation services remain suspended above FL245. Primary risk is anti-aircraft weaponry and military activity; secondary risk is Sudan's proximity to South Sudan, which has poor ATC provision below FL245. Passenger jets have reportedly been targeted by gunfire at HSSK/Khartoum Airport during the conflict.

cross.detail: Following a military coup in April 2023, Sudan remains closed to all civilian flights. There is ongoing fighting between government and militant forces. HSSK/Khartoum airport is closed with no NOTAMs being issued. A Contingency Plan with published overflight routes is available. Several countries advise operators not to enter Sudanese airspace due to risks from anti-aircraft weaponry and military activity. Major events: Nov 2025: Il-76 reportedly shot down by a surface-to-air missile near Babanusa, southern Sudan. May 2025: Drone attack targeting critical infrastructure including HSPN/Port Sudan airport. Oct 2024: Foreign-registered cargo aircraft shot down by local militia over North Darfur, near the border with Chad. Apr 2023: Military coup on Apr 15; Sudan's airspace closed, South Sudan's airspace closed above FL245. Oct 2021: Military coup on Oct 25; HSSK/Khartoum airport closed for two days with all flights suspended.

HLLL.name: FIR Tripoli
HLLL.narrative: Libya's two rival governments and various non-state armed actors create a real risk of misidentification when crossing between areas controlled by different authorities. The one carve-out is for coastal airport approaches made from over the sea. Reliable ATC services cannot be guaranteed, with regular ATS and radar outages and severe VHF limitations across the FIR. Militia have threatened to shoot down civil aircraft operating in western Libya, including at HLLM/Tripoli Mitiga airport. The US has a total flight ban in place; several other countries maintain warnings.
HLLL.restrictionLabel: Do not operate, except flights to coastal airports approached from the sea, subject to ATC contact and your own risk assessment

cross.detail: A civil war has been ongoing since 2014. Libya remains an active conflict zone with armed clashes between rival militia groups. Total flight ban for US operators; several other countries have warnings in place. The primary risk is misidentification by Libyan air-defence systems or militia, who have threatened to shoot down aircraft operating in western Libya including at HLLM/Tripoli Mitiga airport. Military activity has been reported over the high seas operating as OAT or without ATC contact. ATC services are unreliable, with regular outages and severe VHF limitations. Major events: August 2023: Major evacuation of aircraft from Tripoli due to violent clashes and gunfire at Mitiga airport. July 2023: Italy cancelled its 10-year ban on flights to/from Libya. Aug 2022: Militia air-defence forces claimed to have shot down a US drone near Benghazi during increased tensions between competing militias. June 2022: Failed militia attempt to seize government offices in Tripoli; armed clashes resulted in suspension of flights at HLLM/Mitiga airport. Jan 2020: Multiple airstrikes targeting HLLM/Mitiga airport. Nov 2019: Militia advancing on Tripoli declared a no-fly zone around the city, threatening to shoot down civil aircraft attempting to fly to HLLM/Mitiga airport. 2014: HLLT/Tripoli airport closed after clashes between rival militias destroyed most facilities; most flights now operate from HLLM/Mitiga airport.

DRRR.name: Malian territory, especially the north-east
DRRR.conflictType: Insurgency — non-state armed groups active across the Sahel
DRRR.narrative: Non-state armed groups operating in Mali, particularly in the north-east, are assessed to have MANPADS and SAM missile capability, which is why the restriction is altitude-based rather than a total ban. The security situation has escalated sharply as of April 2026, with coordinated nationwide attacks and ongoing sporadic fighting. ATS in Mali is provided by the GOOO/Dakar and DRRR/Niamey FIRs, which maintain a long-standing restriction for overflights of Mali to published ATS routes at FL320 and above.

cross.detail: The conflict in northern and central Mali has continued since 2012 and the security situation remains volatile. Several countries have airspace warnings advising operations at or above FL250 or FL260 and avoiding GATB/Timbuktu, GAGO/Gao and GAKL/Kidal. The US advises caution at all levels due to ongoing fighting, expanding militant activity, and the presence of a state-run paramilitary force operating anti-aircraft systems, military aircraft, UAS and electronic warfare equipment. Primary risks include MANPADS and other surface-to-air weapons, indirect fire near airports, and potential misidentification or spillover from military activity. Low-level and airport-phase operations carry the highest exposure. Major events: April 2026: Security situation escalated sharply. On April 25, coordinated attacks were carried out nationwide against state and military targets, with gunfire and explosions reported near GABS/Bamako. France issued a new airspace warning advising French operators not to operate to/from GABS or use it as an alternate. Sep 2024: Insurgents breached GABS/Bamako and set the presidential jet on fire; multiple attacks occurred across the city and the airport closed temporarily. Dec 2023: Germany prohibited its operators below FL260 in northern Mali. Commercial flights to GATB/Timbuktu cancelled after shelling near the airport; a military jet crashed near GAGO/Gao, with reports it may have been shot down. Aug 2020: All airports closed for two days during a military coup; Bamako ACC remained operational and overflights were unaffected. Apr 2018: Militants attacked UN bases near GATB/Timbuktu using indirect fire and vehicle bombs. Jan 2017 and Nov 2016: Vehicle bomb and rocket attacks targeted GAGO/Gao and GATB/Timbuktu airports.

HCSM.name: Somali airspace
HCSM.conflictType: Insurgency — Al-Shabaab and related terrorist groups
HCSM.narrative: Terrorist organisations operating in Somalia are assessed to have confirmed anti-aircraft weaponry, possibly including MANPADS, driving the same FL260 altitude floor as Mali. From Nov 2025, an authority dispute has emerged in the north: Somaliland has stated all overflights require a PPR from its own CAA, while Somalia has reaffirmed through an AIC that it controls the entire FIR — operators should expect conflicting permit instructions near Hargeisa and northern Somalia. There have also been reports of aircraft within the FIR being contacted by unauthorised ATC units issuing conflicting instructions.

cross.detail: The security situation is highly unstable, with ongoing attacks from extremist militants showing intent to target aviation interests. The primary risk is to overflying aircraft at lower flight levels from anti-aircraft-capable weapons. The US prohibits flights across the HCSM/Mogadishu FIR below FL260 except for flights transiting the overwater portion to/from HDAM/Djibouti airport. Several other countries advise against operating below FL260. A secondary risk comes from unauthorised ATC units issuing conflicting instructions to aircraft in the FIR. From Nov 2025, Somaliland requires PPR from its own CAA for all overflights while Somalia reaffirms control of the entire FIR; expect conflicting permit instructions near Hargeisa and northern Somalia. Major events: Feb 2024: Multiple reports of aircraft in the Mogadishu FIR contacted by a fake controller on frequency issuing conflicting instructions. Aug 2023: Reports of uncontrolled combat helicopters flying at low levels (FL030) without position or routing reports. Oct 2022: Somalian government warned HCMM/Mogadishu airport may be targeted by militant groups. May 2022: Class A airspace implemented in the HCSM/Mogadishu FIR above FL245. 2020–ongoing: Multiple Al-Shabaab attacks on HCMM/Mogadishu and nearby targets including a UN compound. May 2020: An Embraer EMB-120 was shot down on approach to Bardale airstrip, killing all six people on board — an accidental shoot-down by Ethiopian forces combating Al-Shabaab.

OPKR.name: Baluchistan province (partial)
OPKR.conflictType: Insurgency (violent non-state actors) + Kashmir territorial dispute
OPKR.narrative: Violent non-state actor (VNSA) groups with confirmed MANPADS operate in Baluchistan. The Kashmir dispute separately raises misidentification risk further north. Following four days of cross-border strikes between India and Pakistan in May 2025, a ceasefire announced on 10 May has largely held, but the situation remains fragile. Current guidance generally advises operators to remain at or above FL260.

cross.detail: Tensions between Pakistan and India in the disputed Kashmir region, along with longstanding militant activity in parts of western Pakistan, create an ongoing risk in the OPKR/Karachi and OPLR/Lahore FIRs. A ceasefire following the May 2025 escalation has largely held, but military activity could resume with little warning. Several states and EASA maintain altitude-based restrictions rather than full avoidance, generally advising operations at or above FL260. Primary risks are anti-aviation weaponry including potential MANPADS below FL260 and inadvertent risk from military activity or misidentification in the Kashmir region. Major events: Feb 2026: Cross-border strikes between Pakistan and Afghanistan escalated; no new airspace closures issued, and commercial traffic continues to transit OAKX/Kabul FIR via P500 and G500. May 2025: Four days of cross-border strikes and shelling between India and Pakistan in Kashmir; ceasefire announced on 10 May has largely held; some operators temporarily rerouted south via Gulf of Oman and UAE. Jan 2024: Iran conducted missile and drone strikes against a militant group in western Pakistan, highlighting cross-border military activity risk. Dec 2023 – ongoing: Crew reports of GPS spoofing in the OPLR/Lahore FIR area, particularly around OPLA/Lahore. Feb–Aug 2019: Pakistan closed its airspace to overflights following major clashes with India in the Kashmir region.

OPLR.name: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province (partial)
OPLR.conflictType: Insurgency (violent non-state actors) + Kashmir territorial dispute
OPLR.narrative: Covers the north-western province, where the Kashmir dispute adds a misidentification risk on top of the VNSA activity common to both restricted Pakistani provinces. GPS spoofing has been reported in the OPLR/Lahore FIR area, particularly around OPLA/Lahore, since Dec 2023.

cross.detail: Tensions between Pakistan and India in the disputed Kashmir region, along with longstanding militant activity in parts of western Pakistan, create an ongoing risk in the OPKR/Karachi and OPLR/Lahore FIRs. A ceasefire following the May 2025 escalation has largely held, but military activity could resume with little warning. Several states and EASA maintain altitude-based restrictions rather than full avoidance, generally advising operations at or above FL260. Primary risks are anti-aviation weaponry including potential MANPADS below FL260 and inadvertent risk from military activity or misidentification in the Kashmir region. Major events: Feb 2026: Cross-border strikes between Pakistan and Afghanistan escalated; no new airspace closures issued, and commercial traffic continues to transit OAKX/Kabul FIR via P500 and G500. May 2025: Four days of cross-border strikes and shelling between India and Pakistan in Kashmir; ceasefire announced on 10 May has largely held; some operators temporarily rerouted south via Gulf of Oman and UAE. Jan 2024: Iran conducted missile and drone strikes against a militant group in western Pakistan, highlighting cross-border military activity risk. Dec 2023 – ongoing: Crew reports of GPS spoofing in the OPLR/Lahore FIR area, particularly around OPLA/Lahore. Feb–Aug 2019: Pakistan closed its airspace to overflights following major clashes with India in the Kashmir region.

OAKX.name: FIR Kabul
OAKX.conflictType: Post-conflict security vacuum — extremist groups active, limited air traffic services
OAKX.narrative: Since the 2021 Taliban takeover, Afghanistan has had little to no functioning air traffic control. The Kabul FIR is Class G airspace: crews use published contingency routes and TIBA procedures rather than normal ATC clearances. Traffic through the FIR increased in March 2026 as flights sought alternatives to the closed central Middle East corridor. Some countries limit overflights to airways P500 and G500 in the far east of the FIR; others allow overflights across the entire airspace at and above FL320.

cross.detail: March 2026: Afghanistan's airspace (OAKX/Kabul FIR) remains open but has no ATC service. The FIR is uncontrolled Class G airspace following the withdrawal of US and allied forces in Aug 2021. Traffic has increased as flights avoid the closed central Middle East corridor. Overflights must be on specific contingency routes. The primary risk is from surface-to-air fire at low altitudes. There is also no ATC service and an extreme threat to aircraft and crew on the ground. Major events: March 2026: Traffic increases through OAKX/Kabul FIR as flights use the northern bypass route around the closed Middle East corridor. Feb 2026: Cross-border strikes between Pakistan and Afghanistan escalated; commercial traffic continues to transit the FIR including via P500 and G500. Aug 2021: US and allied forces withdrew from Afghanistan; the OAKX/Kabul FIR became uncontrolled Class G airspace with no ATC service.

HAAA.name: FIR Addis Ababa, north of 8.5°N
HAAA.conflictType: Regional/border tension — assessed by EASA as medium risk
HAAA.narrative: This is an EASA Information Note, not a CZIB — meaning EASA's risk assessment group judged the risk here as medium rather than high. Full analytical detail is restricted to the CZ Hub. The primary aviation risk is from large-scale ceasefire violations involving missiles or anti-aircraft weaponry that could threaten overflights, including misidentification or aircraft caught in crossfire. A peace deal in the Tigray region was agreed in Nov 2022, but airspace warnings remain in place from several states.
HAAA.restrictionLabel: Caution only — factor into your own risk assessment and routing, below FL 260

cross.detail: The risk picture in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region (the Ethiopia/Eritrea border) has improved since a peace deal was agreed in Nov 2022, but airspace warnings remain in place from several states. The primary risk is from ceasefire violations involving missiles or anti-aircraft weaponry that may threaten overflights through misidentification or crossfire. Major events: Feb 2024: New flare-up in fighting in the Amhara region (south of Tigray), including air strikes. Nov 2022: Peace deal agreed in the Tigray region; Ethiopian Airlines planning to resume flights to HAMK/Mekele airport. Nov 2021: Several western countries issued airspace and travel warnings for the Tigray region following increased fighting. July 2021: HAAA/Addis FIR published a NOTAM closing a section of airspace below FL290 over the Tigray following reports that militia shot down a military transport plane near Mekele. Nov 2020: Major escalation of conflict in the Tigray region; some airways closed by Ethiopian and Sudanese CAAs. Routes UN321, UG300 and UL432 were very close to the conflict zone. Multiple airports targeted by rockets; missiles fired across the border into Eritrea targeting HHAS/Asmara; HABD/Bahir Dar and HAGN/Gondar also targeted. Sep 2018: Ethiopian ATC controllers went on strike; ECAA and Ethiopian Airlines recruited retired and foreign controllers, some not qualified to operate in Ethiopian airspace. Strike ended Sep 7.

VYYF.name: FIR Yangon, below FL260
VYYF.conflictType: Internal armed conflict — assessed by EASA as medium risk
VYYF.narrative: As with Ethiopia, this is a medium-risk Information Note rather than a do-not-operate CZIB. France's own national guidance goes slightly further operationally, setting a hard altitude floor. The security situation has deteriorated since the military coup in Feb 2021, with air strikes and armed clashes across many parts of the country. GPS jamming has been reported in the north of the FIR on overflights between China and Bangladesh airspace.
VYYF.restrictionLabel: Caution only — factor into your own risk assessment and routing, below FL 260

cross.detail: The security situation in Myanmar has deteriorated since the military coup in Feb 2021. Conflict and violence including air strikes and armed clashes affect many parts of the country. Several countries have issued airspace warnings at lower flight levels due to risk from military operations, surface-to-air fire and anti-aviation weaponry. GPS jamming has been reported in the north of the FIR on overflights between China and Bangladesh airspace. Major events: Jan 2024: Armed group shot down a military helicopter in the northern state of Kachin using a likely MANPAD. Sep 2023: Several attacks by rebel groups against military targets, including a makeshift drone dropping bombs on aircraft hangars at an airbase next to VYNT/Naypyitaw airport. Sep 2023: Reports of intermittent GPS jamming on airway N895 over the mainland in the VYYF/Yangon FIR. Apr 2023: VYYY/Yangon temporarily closed following attack by resistance groups with improvised artillery rounds. Sep 2022: A Myanmar National Airlines passenger was reportedly shot as bullets passed through the fuselage of an ATR 72 on approach to VYLK/Loikaw. Feb 2021: Military coup ousted the government; ATC strike at end of Feb resulted in no ATC service for overflights. Since then, increasing strikes, mass protests, clashes with militia and airstrikes on militia-active areas.
